top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) best meets the common criteria. It pairs a conceptual account of how technology shifts relative labour demand with transparent, replicated local-labour-market designs for import competition, and the work is mature: about three decades for the skill-premium line, two for the task framework and one for the trade-shock papers. The open disputes concern the magnitude and persistence of the effects and shift-share inference, not whether the effects exist. A citation on labour demand, wage structure and local adjustment can treat the two strands as one question without claiming origination of the task framework or restating the 2023 and 2024 citations. Attribution is the weak point: Dorn is excluded by the three-name cap, and Katz's marginal credit is the most exposed because of his work with Goldin. I rank the Dorn variant P002 second because it is a defensible, tighter single-discovery prize. Any B006 configuration is better than no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; my political-science field is not close to B006, and I have no tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn. I note that I am a Stockholm University colleague of Hassler, Krusell and Boppart in a different department.
